On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya was in command, disarming and tying up Sitaram with his own cloth to get past him and save him from the Maharaj's wrath. In contrast, on the night of Udayaditya's prison escape, Sitaram took charge by opening Udayaditya's cell, grabbing and carrying him out of the burning prison, and leading a helpless and disoriented Udayaditya to safety.

Pratapaditya's initial failed plan was to have two Pathan men ambush and kill Basanta Ray while he was traveling to Jessore and taking shelter at an inn in Simultali (which failed when one of the Pathans was charmed by Basanta Ray's music and refused to carry out the murder). 

The method that finally succeeds is when Pratapaditya sends Commander Muktiyar Khan and a group of disguised soldiers to Raigarh fort with a signed execution order; there, a soldier named Abdul kills the old king with a sword while Basanta Ray prostrates and chants prayers before his deity.

1. In the palace inner quarters (the Mahishi's room), disguised as a middle-aged woman.
2. In the king's room at the palace, appearing undisguised as the royal jester.
Mangala (Rukmini) secretly preparing and providing poison disguised as medicine when the Rajmahishi sent Matangini to fetch medicine to win back Udayaditya's heart.
Feeling insulted by her refusal, King Ramchandra Ray decides to take revenge by marrying another wife, leaving Vibha with no place or home in his palace and kingdom when she finally arrives.

After Rukmini obtained Udayaditya's signet ring, Bhagavat and Sitaram used its engraved seal to stamp a forged treasonous petition to the Emperor claiming the kingdom for Udayaditya. Bhagavat then presented the stamped petition to Maharaj Pratapaditya, falsely claiming he had intercepted it from one of Udayaditya's fleeing servants on the way to Delhi, prompting Pratapaditya to order Udayaditya's imprisonment.

During Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya overpowered and tied up the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat, leading Pratapaditya to dismiss them from their posts. When the dismissed guards fell into extreme poverty, Udayaditya provided them with stipends, which Pratapaditya discovered and strictly forbade anyone from continuing. To spare Udayaditya and prevent the families from starving, Surma took over secretly sending the stipends to the guards' families. Once Pratapaditya discovered that Surma was secretly providing these stipends against his orders, he decreed that she be exiled to her father's house.

The emotional significance of the song lies in its expression of deep loneliness, grief, and emptiness—reflecting the sorrow of being left alone, feeling that all one's loved ones are gone and no longer answer one's call, and the loss of joy in singing when those one sang for are no longer present.

Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts:
1. In Raigarh, while sitting peacefully on the veranda of his palace gazing at the setting sun across the fields, missing and yearning to see his distant loved ones in Jessore.
2. In Jessore, amidst the dark, broken reality of the royal palace, while holding Vibha's hand in front of Surma's silent, empty room after learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment and the destruction of the family's happiness.

After failing to stop Udayaditya's escape, Rukmini goes to Pratapaditya and exposes that Udayaditya fled with Basanta Ray to Raigarh. She then leads Pratapaditya's troops and commander Muktiyar Khan directly to Udayaditya in Raigarh, enabling Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers to infiltrate the fort and carry out Pratapaditya's secret death sentence by having Abdul kill Basanta Ray with a sword.

Initially, Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra Ray with cold indifference and aloof superiority—treating the royal family of Chandradwip as utterly insignificant, disregarding musical fanfare or grand welcomes, and casually dismissing him to prioritize state business. In contrast, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status in his own court with active hostility, arrogance, and open mockery—punishing anyone who equates Pratapaditya with him, encouraging daily court sessions where courtiers demean Pratapaditya's lineage as inferior upstarts who once begged his family for royal anointment, and asserting that merely marrying Pratapaditya's daughter was an act of condescension that redeemed Pratapaditya's family.

Living on the outskirts of Jessore under the name Mangala, Rukmini seeks to win Udayaditya's heart and rule Jessore. When the Rajmahishi secretly seeks medicine from her to divert Udayaditya's affections away from his wife, Surma, Rukmini prepares and provides a lethal poison disguised as medicine, which results in Surma's death. Later, Rukmini enters Udayaditya's bedchamber during a storm, manipulating his guilt over their past, demanding his affection, attempting to take Surma's place on his bed, and taking his ring, deeply tormenting the grieving prince.

After being brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner and told he was not worthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya agreed and requested to be released from the throne and allowed to leave for Kashi. The renunciation culminated formally at the temple, where, in front of Pratapaditya, Udayaditya touched the feet of Ma-Kali and swore an oath with Ma-Kali as his witness that he would never accept any part of the kingdom, sit on the throne of Jessore, or touch the royal scepter—leaving Samaraditya as the heir—and invoking the sin of his grand-uncle's murder if he ever broke his vow.

Nayanchand, fearful of Pratapaditya's reaction, brings the letter to the Mahishi (Vibha's mother) instead of Pratapaditya. To protect Vibha and ensure she returns to Chandradwip without objection, Basanta Ray advises the Mahishi to conceal the true contents, and the Mahishi subsequently announces to Vibha and the household that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house.

Although Pratapaditya had the canal adjoining the palace blocked with large Sal wood logs, Rammohan and his followers pulled Ramchandra Ray's boat up and over the logs, and the pursuing guards were too disorganized and delayed in fetching weapons and a chase boat to stop them.

Basanta Ray's despair is reflected when his emotional turmoil and tears overwhelm him to the point that he can no longer play his sitar, ultimately leading him to leave it behind with Udayaditya and declare he will play it no more. Later, separated from his "eternal companion," he somberly states that while he still has the sitar, its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned, symbolizing his complete loss of joy and music without his loved ones.

Previously, Udayaditya had the courage to treat danger as a trifle, fight oppression with all his might, involve himself in his subjects' affairs, and intervene to protect subjects from royal officials without considering the consequences. After Surma's death, he lost his courage and became gripped by a blind fear of Pratapaditya, hesitating and failing to act—such as turning back after ordering a horse to stop an attack on a zamindar's estate office, running into his house when a beaten subject begged him for mercy, and failing to send financial help to those in hardship.
He helps Udayaditya escape from prison during a fire by opening his cell door, leading him out, and taking him to safety.

On the first occasion, Rammohan created a rope from thick sheets tied to a roof pillar, carried Ramchandra Ray on his back as he climbed down the rope toward the canal, gripped the rope with his teeth at the bottom to carefully lower Ramchandra into a boat with both hands, and then jumped down. 

On the second occasion, after Vibha fainted onto the floor, Rammohan lifted her, carried her out of the palace, placed her into a palanquin near the palace gate, and returned with her to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is elaborately and lavishly adorned in royal splendor by her mother, wearing eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a heavily styled coiffure. In contrast, when she seeks Ramchandra Ray out in Chandradwip, she refuses a royal palanquin and dresses as a common woman, entering the palace on foot like a maidservant and appearing so humble and unadorned that the king mistakes her for a beggar woman seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death, the window symbolizes grief, longing, and the painful absence of Surma, serving as a place where he leaves her spot empty and harbors a lingering hope of seeing her sitting there again. In the prison cell, the window transforms into a symbol of natural freedom and liberation, where looking at the open sky and flying birds reminds him that he is naturally free, that no ruler can truly hold him captive, and that his cage and chains will one day break.

Initially, Sitaram visits Rukmini to borrow money using playful banter, romantic verses, and affectionate pet names, while Rukmini indulgently lends him cash. 

Their dynamic fractures when Udayaditya is imprisoned. Sitaram storms into Rukmini's house, curses her, almost strikes her, and threatens to burn her home, grind her face into the stone floor, and drive her out of the city, inciting deep rage and mutual hostility over their loyalties to the Yubaraj.

The hostility culminates in a life-threatening encounter after Sitaram orchestrates Udayaditya's escape and prison fire. Believing Rukmini is dead, Sitaram sneaks into her cottage to steal her money before fleeing the city. Finding her alive, wet, and shivering in the dark, she furiously vows to burn him and the Yubaraj on a pyre. When Sitaram tries to placate her by feigning his old affectionate charm, Rukmini is enraged to the point of fetching a curved blade to kill him. Recognizing the real danger to his life, Sitaram flees just before Rukmini returns and repeatedly hacks at the empty floor where he had been standing.

Initially, Sitaram uses the fire in the guards' huts as a distraction to draw the guards away from their posts so he can sneak Udayaditya out of his cell and onto an escape boat. To turn it into a full-fledged cover-up, Sitaram returns and has his men set fire to Udayaditya's empty prison cell. He throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning room, while he and his accomplices raise false alarms that Udayaditya was heard screaming and that the roof collapsed on him, staging the scene to make it appear that the Yubaraj died in the fire.

Ramchandra Ray felt no gratitude toward Udayaditya, believing that Udayaditya had only saved him for the sake of his own sister (Vibha) rather than with the primary objective of saving Ramchandra's life. He also felt that it was only natural for everyone to unite to save him from peril, and he joined his courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya simply for being Pratapaditya's son.

Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition bearing Prince Udayaditya's seal to make it appear that the Prince is lodging a treason complaint against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi to claim the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat then presents this forged petition directly to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted it while Udayaditya's servant was carrying it to Delhi.

During Surma's life, Vibha would secretly go to her to have her hair styled to her own liking when her mother's styling was unbearable. Following Surma's tragic absence, Vibha sits waiting quietly at hair-braiding time expecting Surma to arrive, only for evening to fall and night to approach with her hair left unbraided and unkempt, marking the void left by Surma's absence and lack of care.
